title: Slab Sundial Workshop
pitch: The visitor carves a virtual granite sundial: picks a city, tilts the dial plate, sets the gnomon, and watches hour lines and a live shadow appear. Scrubbing the calendar makes the shadow tip trace its yearly figure-eight, and a 'Dial vs Watch' round asks them to read the shadow, guess what the wall clock says, then see why the two disagree by a different amount every week. Each round ends in an itemised correction receipt (longitude, equation of time, the daylight-saving hour) that is the screenshot moment.
whyNow: US clocks fall back on Sunday 2026-11-01 and UK/EU clocks on Sunday 2026-10-25, so the gap between sun time and wall time is about to jump by an hour while autumn sunsets race earlier. The mechanic is astronomy, so it stays good in March and in any season.

research.summary: As of 2026-10-10, several independent outlets agree US daylight saving ends Sunday 2026-11-01 at 2 a.m. local time, and UK/EU summer time ends Sunday 2026-10-25. Independent pages (timeanddate, public radio) explain that the earliest sunset of the year falls before the winter solstice because sundial time and clock time drift apart (the equation of time). That gives the page a true, checkable surprise to teach: the shadow, the longitude offset, the equation of time and the daylight-saving hour are separate corrections stacked on one wall clock. All astronomy is computed in the page from standard low-precision formulas, so no download is needed; only a small hand-made city table (rounded coordinates plus clock rule) is bundled and labelled approximate.

title: Small Sample Rink
pitch: The 84-game NHL season opened on 2026-09-29, so every fan is currently staring at records like 3-0-1. The visitor dials in a fictional team's start and games played, and a worker grows an orchard of thousands of simulated seasons, each one a fruit hanging at its final point total, so the spread shows what a hot or cold start really means. A 'regression receipt' itemises how many points of the start are likely luck, and a Call the Season game scores the visitor's gut against the simulation.
whyNow: The season opened 2026-09-29 and is a record 84 games per team, so early-season hot takes are everywhere this week. The sampling mechanic works on any season length and any start, so it stays useful all winter.

research.summary: As of 2026-10-10, the NHL's own news pages and ESPN report that the 2026-27 regular season began Tuesday 2026-09-29 and is a league-record 84 games per team (1,344 games total, ending 2027-04-10). Two independent explainers agree on the points rule (2 for a win, 1 for an overtime or shootout loss, 0 for a regulation loss, in place since 1999-2000), which creates the extra variance the simulator needs to model. One analytics write-up (single source, unverified) reports that after the first month, teams in the top 10 by points percentage made the playoffs far more often than the bottom 10 over 2014-15 to 2023-24, which frames the 'how much does a start tell you' question. The model is deliberately fictional: invented teams, adjustable talent and overtime assumptions, all labelled as simulation rather than league data.

title: Seven Riffles
pitch: A night-shift dealer swears three riffles is plenty. The visitor shuffles a drawn 52-card deck with a hand-made riffle (cut, then release), watches 'rising sequences' fan out like strands, and sees an exact meter of how far the deck still sits from truly random. Then they audit: run ten million seeded shuffles at 1 to 10 riffles and watch the chart show 'new deck order' and 'sorted suits' survive until the shuffle count nears seven.
whyNow: Timeless: the seven-shuffles slogan is half-known and widely misquoted, and it is a good argument to lose. Nothing similar has shipped.

research.summary: The Gilbert-Shannon-Reeds model cuts a deck at a binomially distributed point and interleaves the two piles with probability proportional to pile sizes. Bayer and Diaconis showed the chance of any deck order after m riffles depends only on its number of rising sequences, so the distance from uniform for 52 cards can be computed EXACTLY (no sampling) and compared with Monte Carlo. Distance stays near 1 for about four to five riffles, then collapses (cutoff), and is under 0.5 at seven. The slogan depends on the metric: an entropy-based argument by other authors says five to six may do. That argument is the game: the visitor picks a yardstick and watches the verdict change. The uniqueness of every well-mixed deck (52 factorial is about 8.07e67) gives the closing line.

title: Second Pick Wins
pitch: Choose a three-flip coin pattern; a smug bot picks its own after seeing yours, and a flip-by-flip race decides who sees their pattern first. The visitor loses far more than half the time, for any pattern they try, then cranks the race to ten million flips and watches the bot's edge settle on exact fractions like 2 to 1, and finally flips the table by taking the second pick themselves. A red-and-black card mode with tricks turns the cascade of flips into a visible deck.
whyNow: Timeless. The result is a clean argument-loser: the game is fair in each pick yet rigged by order of choice, and nothing like it has shipped.

research.summary: In Penney's game two players each pick a short heads-tails pattern and the one that appears first in a fair coin sequence wins. Because picking is sequential, the second picker can always choose a reply that beats the first pick; for every three-flip pattern a better reply exists. A short rule builds the reply, and Conway's leading-number method gives exact odds. A card version (red/black cards, collecting tricks) exists. The page can show the full payoff matrix of lengths 3 to 5, the exact Markov-chain odds next to a ten-million-flip seeded Monte Carlo, and expected waiting times, where the winning pattern is not always the quicker one on average, which is what makes the loss feel unfair.

title: Culture Plate
pitch: A glowing petri dish under a blacklight holds a live Gray-Scott reaction-diffusion culture. The visitor inoculates it with a fingertip, then steers its chemistry by dragging a marker across a hand-labelled feed/kill map whose regions are named like pantry items (spots, worms, coral, bubbling, mitosis). A slow drift mode lets the culture ferment from one regime to the next, and a poster mode stamps the result with a museum-style specimen label and a shareable seed.
whyNow: Timeless: reaction-diffusion is the most photogenic bit of mathematics on the web, and an autumn-dark ultraviolet palette with a lab-specimen framing gives it a point of view that differs from the stock demos.

research.summary: Gray-Scott is a two-chemical model on a grid: chemical A is fed in at rate f, chemical B is removed at rate k, and B converts A. Per Karl Sims's tutorial, a 3x3 Laplacian with weights -1 centre, 0.2 edges, 0.05 corners (summing to zero) is enough, and typical values are DA=1.0, DB=0.5, f=0.055, k=0.062. The (f, k) plane is a known map of regimes: spots, stripes, waves, worms, solitons, solid regions. Exact coordinates differ between implementations (grid size, step, diffusion constants), so the page will calibrate its own map and label presets as this page's calibration. Prior art exists (Sims's RD Tool, a Google experiment, a Frankfurt applet), so the value lies in the point of view: the named map, drift mode, contamination brush, specimen-label poster and shareable seed. Model limits: a toy two-species chemistry on a flat grid, not real fermentation; Turing-type mechanisms are plausible for fish pigment stripes but evidence elsewhere (for example digits) is mostly simulation-based.

title: Unreliable Plotter
pitch: A virtual pen plotter draws a generative poster line by line on screen: flow-field ribbons, L-system shrubs or spiral-packed circles, each in two or three pens. The twist is a mishap dial that lets the machine misbehave in physically motivated ways (a pen drying out and skipping, a blot on touchdown, paper creeping between pen swaps), narrated by a deadpan operator log. The visitor hunts for the dial setting where the imperfections make the poster better than the ideal version, then shares the seed or saves the layered SVG.
whyNow: Timeless: pen-plotter flow-field art is a recognised craft scene, and treating machine error as a creative parameter is a fresh angle on a familiar genre.

research.summary: A flow field is a grid of direction vectors, usually angles taken from Perlin noise, along which particles are traced to produce smooth curves; the technique is widely used and suits plotters because each curve is one continuous pen stroke. Plotter workflows separate artwork into SVG layers that map to pens. The mishap model is stylised: ordinary pens skip when the tip clogs or the paper is rough or very absorbent, and one forum report describes paper drifting during long plots, but none of this is calibrated to a specific machine. The page therefore labels the physics as an approximation and keeps the ideal SVG export honest. Perlin noise was formally described in a 1985 SIGGRAPH paper; sources disagree on whether it was first developed in 1982 or 1983, so the page leaves that date out.

title: Cabinet of Opinions
pitch: A deadpan product page, control panel and manual for an invented smart filing cabinet whose drawers slam shut according to a secret rule. The visitor feeds it absurd little documents, watches which drawer it picks, and deduces the rule from the slams and the cryptic manual; then a tide gauge turns and the cabinet silently switches rules, so the second minute is about noticing you are being stubborn. A seeded daily rule set and a shareable result card make the tenth minute different from the first.
whyNow: Timeless. Hidden-rule deduction games are well loved and rare on the web, and wrapping one in a product-page parody makes the rule the punchline.

research.summary: Two established hidden-rule formats shape the mechanic: a Zendo-style game where a master's rule is inferred from marked examples, and the Wisconsin card sorting task where the sorting rule changes without warning and the main measure is clinging to the old rule. The tide gauge borrows the real roughly 12 h 25 min semidiurnal tide period as the cycle on which the cabinet swaps rules. Filing-cabinet history (disputed invention, Library Bureau a leading name) supplies the fictional company's mock heritage page. Parody-genre sources say the humour comes from a deadpan narrator who reveals too much, which fixes the voice. No real company or product is parodied; the genre of product pages is.

title: The Overtoaster
pitch: The product page, control panel and manual of an invented heater-grid toaster that burns pictures onto bread, with a real two-stage heat and moisture simulation underneath. The visitor sets power per heating cell, watches the slice dry out first and only then brown, and tries to match a daily target design without charring the crust, while the product's absurd subscription tiers and pop-ups pester the page in the margins. The finished slice is a screenshot-ready piece of burnt art with a deadpan review.
whyNow: Timeless. Appliances that hide features behind paywalls and apps are a lasting genre to lampoon, and a toaster is the oldest joke in connected gadgets.

research.summary: Food-science and patent sources agree on the physics that shapes the mechanic: bread surface water holds the surface near 100 C, so toasting is a drying stage followed by browning, and browning chemistry is reported to start somewhere from about 120 to 155 C depending on the source. That makes the simulator two coupled fields (moisture and temperature) with a latent-heat plateau, so patience visibly matters. Real patents and older gadgets already print or select browning patterns, so the page is a genre parody rather than a novelty claim. Consumer-group and tech-press pieces on features locked behind subscriptions justify the satirical tier-and-pop-up layer, which targets the practice, not any company.

title: The Wrong Window
pitch: The visitor is a citizen inside a tiny invented Ministry of nine counters, holding one goal (for example, a Licence to Keep One Goose) and a pocket of forms. Each counter's rulebook entry is a readable rule about what it wants, what it stamps and when it closes, and the visitor plans a route, queues, gets sent to the other department, and slowly discovers loopholes that emerge when rules combine (a photocopier that clones stamps, a pneumatic underpass between floors, a clerk who relaxes for cake). A daily seed, a shareable route receipt covered in tilted ink stamps, and a count of loopholes found make the second and tenth run feel different.
whyNow: Timeless. The Papers, Please style of rule-reading puzzle has stayed popular for years, and a warm, fictional, no-politics version with composable rules and a built-in solver is an open niche.

research.summary: The genre anchor is the document-checking puzzle where a rulebook grows day by day and the tension comes from speed against accuracy, with the bureaucratic frame making it easy to author many gameplay rules. Small stamp-and-deliver jam games exist, but in the one seen the order of stamping does not matter, so a game where rules compose, order matters and a solver proves solvability and finds unintended shortcuts is a different design. Cultural material for the jokes is real and checkable: Catch-22 as a loop of mutually dependent rules, red tape as the literal ribbon once used to bind official papers, and Parkinson's satirical laws of officials making work for each other. Every agency, clerk and form in the page is invented.

title: Clause And Effect
pitch: The visitor is the lone clerk of an Amendments Desk facing a knot of red tape: offices drawn as nodes, requirements as strands, and queues of citizens stuck because permit A needs B and B needs A. With a small budget of amendment clauses (an exemption, a sunset clause, a grandfather clause, a deemed-approved-after-N-days rule, a brand-new office) the visitor pulls strands loose and then runs a simulated crowd through the system, watching who still gets stuck. Parkinson-style side effects punish lazy fixes, since every new office spawns paperwork for its neighbours, so the tidiest unravelled desk wins.
whyNow: Timeless. It turns a real piece of computer science (deadlock and circular wait) into a joke-rich puzzle that rewards seeing the structure of a mess.

research.summary: Deadlock theory gives the puzzle a precise spine: a system can deadlock only when four conditions hold together, circular wait among them, and the standard cures (break a condition, impose an ordering on resources) map neatly onto bureaucratic amendments. Where each resource has a single instance, a cycle in the wait graph means deadlock, so a strongly-connected-component pass can show the player exactly which knot is the Catch-22. Parkinson's satirical observation that the number of officials grows regardless of the work supplies the side-effect rule that stops brute-force fixing. All offices, permits and citizens are invented.

title: Jokers In Phase
pitch: A concept mod for a poker roguelike: a new joker family whose bonuses depend on timing instead of just position. A Pendulum joker swings between flat mult and multiplied mult hand by hand, Firefly jokers blink on their own beat and slowly nudge their neighbours into step, and Handshake jokers pay out only when the two jokers beside them are in matching phase. The visitor arranges a five-slot rail, plays seeded hands through a tiny chips-times-mult engine, and watches a phase ring show who is in sync; a fully synchronised rail makes the whole page pulse once and drops a screenshot-worthy score card.
whyNow: Timeless for the modding community: joker ordering is the core puzzle of the genre and no vanilla joker cares about rhythm, so the family opens a new axis of play. The page is a self-contained sandbox that works offline, so it stays good for weeks.

research.summary: Community guides agree on the evaluation rule that makes joker order matter: effects resolve left to right, with flat mult before multiplying mult. That ordering is the hook the new family bends: instead of only where a joker sits, when it fires also changes its value. The mod scene already runs on a common loader and injector pair, and mod listings show that vanilla-feeling joker packs are what many modders aim for, so the concept ships with a rail that mimics that scale. All scoring numbers in the page are invented for the concept and labelled as such.

title: Blind Foundry

research.summary: Boss blinds in the source game attack a specific plan (for example banning repeated hand types, limiting a round to one hand type, debuffing a suit, or forcing five-card hands), which is why they are a favourite mod target: several community mods list dozens of new ones. Balance for scoring-multiplier games is hard because stacking can produce runaway combos, and sources on the genre say heavy playtesting is required, so a quick in-browser Monte Carlo of simple bots is a genuine, useful stand-in for a designer's first pass. The lab uses invented numbers and toy bots, clearly labelled, and the exact vanilla blind rules are shown only as 'per fan guides' because they were not confirmed against the developer's own text.

title: The Waiting Hum
pitch: A calm little waiting room whose arrivals and departures are played as soft notes: run it at low load and it sounds like a slow lullaby, push the load toward capacity and the tune swells, stutters and collapses into a tangle. The visitor staffs the counters, chooses one shared line or separate lines, and tunes how erratic arrivals and service are, trying to keep the average wait under a target on a budget. A live panel compares the running simulation with the textbook formulas, so the famous knee in the waiting-time curve is something you hear and see.
whyNow: Timeless. Queue theory is the textbook definition of a dud subject, rescued by letting the visitor hear a system approach saturation.

research.summary: Standard university sources agree on the M/M/1 results (mean number in system rho/(1-rho), time 1/(mu-lambda), both diverging as utilization approaches 1) and on Little's law holding regardless of distributions. Kingman's approximation adds a variability term that lets the page show why erratic arrivals or service inflate waits. Operations writing supports the pooled single line for reducing wait variability while noting people prefer it partly for fairness. Parameter-mapping sonification is an established technique with a known caution about quantizing to scales. The sim computes truth; the formulas run alongside as a check.

title: Starter Pack Syntax
pitch: The visitor is dealt a subject card for a thing rather than a person (a rainy Monday, a rink snack bar at the second intermission, a first week with a new roguelike) and fills a cobblestone-style mosaic of six tiles from a tray of hand-drawn vector items. A live grammar linter labels every tile with its job (the unmistakable anchor, the niche specific, the filler, the ironic turn) and scores the pack on balance, recognisability and sting. A reverse mode shows a finished pack and asks which subject it was; any pack exports as a PNG and as a shareable link.
whyNow: The starter pack is a Reddit-born format that has stayed active for years, so the grammar is timeless; the page also takes a seasonal subject deck keyed to the run date. I could not verify a single format that dominates this particular week (trend lists disagree), so the hook is the structure, not a news item.

research.summary: The starter pack is a well-documented, Reddit-centred collage format: a plain title plus a handful of images that together stand for a stereotype or situation. Wikipedia and Know Your Meme both trace it to a late September 2014 Twitter post, and the community later split off derivative templates where one image is swapped. Linguists have started treating memes as having rules of composition (labelled-object templates, multimodal grammar), which supports a page that makes the slots and roles explicit. Every subject in the page is a thing or situation, never a group of people or a private person, and all art is drawn in code. Trend lists for early October 2026 come from marketing blogs and do not agree on one dominant format, so no news claim is made.

title: Format Drift
pitch: The visitor writes one tiny joke into an original drawn template (a two-panel contrast, an escalating four-tier ladder, a three-figure triangle or a plan-goes-wrong strip) and releases it into a simulated gossip chain. Each retelling mutates the joke in a small, named way (a role swap, an extra rung, an ironic flip, a literalised word, a topic substitution), growing a layered tree of variants whose edit distance from the original is shown on every branch. The visitor then acts as the audience and chooses which variants survive to be retold, steering the lineage until the final descendant is barely recognisable beside the original.
whyNow: Timeless rather than news-bound: published studies reconstruct descent trees of meme variants, and the expanding-brain ladder and three-figure labelling formats are still reused constantly. Evolution as a toy is novel for the studio and gives a screenshot-worthy side-by-side of ancestor and descendant.

research.summary: Researchers have repeatedly modelled memes as things that mutate when copied. A study of thousands of Facebook meme variants builds ancestor-to-descendant trees and reports that edit distance grows along copy chains, while two other arXiv papers build trees of image-macro variants and a dendrogram of frog-meme clusters. The expanding-brain format started in a Reddit joke called Whomst and is a four-image escalation; the three-figure labelling format has role slots that people relabel for any topic. Those documented structures become the mutation operators. The simulation is invented and labelled as such; it does not claim to reproduce any measurement.

facts.claim: Published studies arrange meme variants as descent trees or dendrograms built from pairwise distances (Facebook meme study, MemeSequencer, frog-meme clustering).
The Facebook meme study reports that variants further apart in a copy chain differ more in edit distance, and notes the biological analogy is only partly established.
The expanding-brain ladder began as an escalating four-image series from the Whomst joke, as covered by both Know Your Meme and Dictionary.com.
As of 2026-10-10, per Know Your Meme, the escalating-brain format is often used ironically to imply the opposite of its literal ranking (single source, shown as reported).
The three-figure labelling format has role slots (the person, the current focus, the tempting alternative) that are relabelled for arbitrary topics.

design.coreLoop: Write a seed joke into a template, release it for three retellings, read each new variant with its mutation named, pick survivors, and repeat for up to eight generations. Operators interact (an irony flip after an extra rung reads differently from before), the tree shows divergence at a glance, and players learn which mutation each template is most vulnerable to.
sophisticationHooks: Five or six named mutation operators acting on structured slots: role swap, add rung, drop rung, irony flip, literalise, topic substitute via a hand-made neighbour graph of about 150 concepts
Selection pressure: the visitor's pick decides survivors; an auto-select 'algorithmic feed' mode favours the most extreme variants and visibly collapses diversity, to show what selection does
Layered tree view as a canopy of nodes, each a mini rendered panel, with edit distance on each edge and a final ancestor-versus-descendant side-by-side card
Original art only: four stick-figure and glyph templates drawn in SVG, with URL-hash state holding template, seed words and the chosen path so lineages are shareable
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: four templates, the operator engine with seeded random so hashes replay exactly, the concept neighbour graph and ladder dataset (about 25 ladders of four rungs), tree and side-by-side views, feed-mode toggle, keyboard navigation, light and dark, reduced motion, about panel listing only verified sources and labelling the simulation as invented. Cut: free-form text mutation, image upload, real templates or photos, any claim of measured accuracy.
risks: Quality of mutated text depends on the hand-made graph and ladders; the engine should degrade to structure-only mutations when typed words are unknown
Mutations may yield flat jokes; mitigate by curating operator outputs with templates tested on the 25 ladders before the build freeze
The page must say clearly that the simulation is invented and not a replication of the cited studies
Know Your Meme irony claim is single-source and is shown only as 'per Know Your Meme' if at all
The three-figure template is described by original drawings, never the stock photo or any real person
